prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My position is unchanged and the first round has made me more confident in it. The decisive physical step is simple enough to draw on a blackboard: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts the two clock levels by the same amount, so the atoms can be held tightly, which removes Doppler and recoil effects, without moving the transition. That is what separates the lattice clock from both earlier prizes. The 2005 comb prize gave us the means to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize concerned control of a single trapped quantum system, whose signal is small and whose stability is limited by one particle. The lattice clock lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated together, which is where the stability comes from, and it brought in many-body effects such as collisions and spin exchange that now have to be understood in the clock itself. Different laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and overtaken one another near 1e-18, so the result does not rest on one measurement, and the agreement between independent clocks is exactly the theory-experiment precision I trust. The reach into fundamental physics is concrete: gravitational redshift across millimetres, limits on drifting constants, dark-matter couplings, and the preparation of a new definition of the second. Five of eight members now prefer this two-name configuration, from atomic physics, particle physics, condensed matter and instrumentation, and none argues against its scientific standing. I do not count heads as a substitute for judgement, but I note that the objections raised are about novelty and priority, which are testable, and not about the physics. A citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice answers the novelty point directly.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, a sceptic can still call this a spectacular refinement of optical frequency standards, so the citation must carry the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom interrogation and must not read as a second comb prize. Second, priority beyond the two names is not verified. From my own memory of the record, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock come from Katori's group in 2001-2005, while the accuracy, stability and many-body programme and the first 1e-18 systematic evaluations come from Ye's group at JILA, but Lemonde and colleagues at SYRTE, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley and others made important contributions that I cannot rank without the documents. If a check shows that one of them stands on equal footing with Katori or Ye, a two-name prize would be wrong and I would want that said openly. Third, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, and the strongest applications (clock-based dark-matter and gravitational-wave searches, relativistic geodesy) are still prospective. I weigh that last point lightly, since prizes have honoured instruments before their largest uses arrived, but I understand why Johansson and Kroll raise it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B031 eighth and prefers B024, saying that the magic-wavelength idea refines a measurement line already honoured in 2005 and 2012, whereas moire flat bands opened a new class of correlated matter; he accepts that Katori and Ye are the natural pair and the clocks mature.
responses.response: The chair asks you whether novelty is your only objection, and I would like to answer the novelty point on its merits. The comb and the single-ion work do not solve the problem the lattice clock solves: holding a very large number of neutral atoms without perturbing the transition. Without the magic wavelength the trap itself would destroy the accuracy, so this is a new idea and not a better number, and it created a regime where the clock is a many-body system. I would also say that fundamental-physics reach counts as discovery for me, since a clock that sees a gravitational redshift across a millimetre is a new instrument for testing relativity. I respect the elegance of the Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism and I agree that flat bands are a real discovery. My reservation about B024 is not its merit but its timing and the incomplete experimental credit, and if you could accept B031 as your second choice I think that would be the most natural convergence, though I do not ask you to move on a head count.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the unresolved pairing mechanism is only a detail of one phase of twisted bilayer graphene and not a maturity problem, noting that high-temperature superconductivity was recognised before its mechanism was understood, and asks how decisive the lattice-clock step is relative to the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is fair, and I accept that a mechanism does not have to be settled for a discovery to be recognised. I have changed my mind slightly on how I put it: I would no longer say that the pairing question alone makes B024 premature. What still holds me back, as a non-specialist in condensed matter, is that the experimental first author of the 2018 papers lies outside any three-name credit while the theory side needs all three of the names you propose, so the configuration is incomplete on the experimental side. That is a limit of the rule and not of the science, and it argues for waiting to see whether the field settles it. On your question to me: the step beyond 2005 is that the comb counts the cycles while the lattice makes a clock whose stability comes from interrogating thousands of atoms with the trap shifts cancelled. I would not oppose B024 if the room moved there, and I keep it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Kroll supports B031 with a citation about the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and says that he sees Katori as the origin of the magic-wavelength idea and first demonstrations and Ye as the one who delivered the extreme performance, with the priority split recalled from memory.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the credit, and I now think we should say plainly in the citation that this is a shared invention and realisation. I also want to hold us to a check that we have so far only asked for. Both of us have said we recall the Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates contributions from memory. Before the final ballot I would want the committee to confirm that the proposal and first demonstration come from Katori and that the first evaluations at the 1e-18 level and the many-body programme come from Ye. If that record holds, I think the limit to two names is defensible and the case is stronger than any alternative on the list. If it does not, we should say so and not rely on the clean attribution that several of us have been repeating.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength trapping idea so the prize is not read as a second comb prize, and notes that combining B031 with B009 would need five names, so a two-part prize is not available within the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree with both points and have changed my citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom trapping explicitly. On the second part, I considered adding one and came down against it. B009 would need Rose, Urban and Haider, and with Katori and Ye that makes five names. The Krivanek question you and Eriksson raised also leaves the credit unsettled. Adding a second part only to reach for a pairing would, I think, dilute a clean single-achievement prize that the committee can defend in one sentence. I would be glad to see B009 return in a later year with the priority question resolved.

responses.point: Pearce, now a B031 supporter, keeps B005 as his first alternative and asks the committee to consider how the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize and the 2023, 2012 and 2005 atomic and optical prizes should weigh against candidates from the same area this year.
responses.response: I do not think the earlier prizes should weigh against B031. The 2023 attosecond prize, which I know from the inside through my work with Anne L'Huillier and others, concerned light pulses and electron dynamics, and the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. Neither covers the physics of atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, so I do not see a repeat. The only version of your point that I take seriously is the 2005 and 2012 overlap with lattice clocks, which I have answered above. On B005, I repeat that the science is first-rate and beyond dispute and that I defer to you and Danielsson on particle physics. My difficulty is that four members proposed three different trios, and the committee has not found a rule for choosing among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee. If Danielsson can state such a rule I would listen, but I would not put it above the clock this year.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second and questions whether a precision-measurement instrument is a discovery in the sense of Nobel's will, while holding that the clock opened genuinely new physics and that the Katori and Ye credit is clean.
responses.response: I would not wait for the redefinition. It is a decision of the metrology community that depends on the committees for time and frequency and on several clock types, so it is not a scientific test of the invention. The science is already established by the independent agreement at 1e-18 and by the millimetre redshift measurement. On discovery versus instrument, I think the useful test is whether the instrument reveals physics that was not accessible before, and for the lattice clock it does, in the many-body shifts inside the clock and the sensitivity to constants and dark matter. I also agree with you on B028: it is my first alternative, but until the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger and Cirac is settled without a contested split, it cannot be my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record outside Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley) is consistent with a two-name prize; I have not verified it from documents and ask for the check before the final ballot.

Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I think the magic-wavelength idea and many-atom interrogation make it so, but Mehlig disagrees and I cannot prove it to him.
How much the pending redefinition of the second should matter; I judge it a matter of timing, not of scientific merit.
I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on whether twisted bilayer graphene will look mature in a few years, and to Danielsson and Pearce on the Higgs attribution.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. None of the credited names for B031 (Katori, Ye) is among my collaborators, so no specific recusal conflict arises for this candidate. I work in the same broad atomic-physics community as the clock and cold-atom candidates (B031, B028), and I ask that this proximity remain on record. I have no ties to the ATLAS, CMS, graphene or electron-microscopy candidates.
